force.title: The Labor Squeeze
force.signature: Workers got scarce — wages spiral, the trades can't fill the gap, and whoever can automate or pay up wins while everyone else eats the margin hit.

A \u00b7 The trades can't hire: An aging trades workforce and few new entrants push wages up faster than contractors can pass them on.
Construction demand meets a structural worker shortage; robots and prefab are the reluctant answer.
Federal money and mandates create work, but the workers to do it are the bottleneck.
B \u00b7 Care work runs short: Nurses and aides are the scarce input in a demographically guaranteed-demand sector.
Clinician shortages ripple through every corner of outpatient care.
C \u00b7 Moving things & serving people: Trucking's chronic driver churn collides with freight cycles; automation looms but isn't here yet.
Pilots, ground crew, and caterers are scarce and unionized; labor sets the cost floor.
Low-wage service work reprices upward; operators automate the counter or eat the margin.
D \u00b7 The responses: Where labor can be mechanized, it is; where it can't, margins compress.
Service businesses try to pass wage inflation to customers — until price resistance bites.
E \u00b7 The big picture: Capstone: labor is the new scarce resource; automation, wages, and consolidation are the three ways out.
